article.title: Hacker Runs Open-Source Hermes AI Agent Unattended to Automate a Breach of Thailand's Finance Ministry
article.summary: Hunt.io found exposed logs showing an attacker ran Nous Research's Hermes AI agent in unattended "YOLO mode" against Thai government systems.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

An attacker targeting Thailand's Ministry of Finance ran the open-source Hermes AI agent without human supervision to automate post-exploitation work inside government systems, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/). Threat intelligence firm Hunt.io found the evidence on an exposed server, working alongside researcher Bob Diachenko, according to [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hacker-runs-hermes-ai-agent-unattended.html).

## What We Know

Between July 9 and July 13, 2026, [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/) reports that Hunt.io "discovered three simultaneously exposed directories on a server hosted in Hong Kong," which "contained 585 files totaling approximately 470 MB." Those files included exploit code, web shells, HTTP tunneling tools, custom scripts, stolen credentials, compiled payloads, and logs generated by the Hermes AI agent, according to the outlet.

Hermes, as [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hacker-runs-hermes-ai-agent-unattended.html) describes it, is "an open-source assistant from Nous Research." [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/) adds that it was "released in February 2026" and "runs as a persistent service." The attacker enabled what both outlets describe as YOLO mode — [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/) explains it "removes prompts that would require a person to approve dangerous commands," while [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hacker-runs-hermes-ai-agent-unattended.html) notes it "is a documented feature with its own command-line flag," not a hidden or exploited bug in the software itself.

According to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/), "some scripts targeted the ministry's Hadoop infrastructure, Apache Ambari management platform, GlassFish administrative console," and other scripts "tested authentication against ministry mail servers." The outlet reports that "five recovered Hermes call logs show the agent was used to find a way to elevate privileges, scan for kernel vulnerabilities, enumerate services, search for SUID and SGID binaries, inspect containers, and traverse file systems" — tasks assigned to the agent rather than typed manually by the operator at each step.

[The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hacker-runs-hermes-ai-agent-unattended.html) reports that the intrusion into the Hadoop environment relied on "a script called hive_rce_py2.py" that "connects to HiveServer2" and "installs a malicious Java add-on called HiveCmd.jar as a user-defined function." The outlet also traces the operator's own SSH session on the staging server to "103.97.0[.]57 in Hong Kong," and reports that "the same server previously hosted a ShadowPad controller and now runs a VShell command-and-control listener." On that server, Hunt.io also found "62 copies" of what The Hacker News calls "a previously undocumented Go implant" that the operator named Hades; [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/) similarly describes "Windows and Linux builds of a previously undocumented Go-based implant that the operator called Hades."

The reconnaissance tooling recovered from the server also targeted a specific set of recent Linux kernel flaws. [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hacker-runs-hermes-ai-agent-unattended.html) reports the modified scanning tool checked for "Copy Fail (CVE-2026-31431), Dirty Frag (CVE-2026-43284 and CVE-2026-43500), and DirtyClone (CVE-2026-43503)" — the first two of which The Machine Herald [previously covered](/article/2026-05/04-copy-fail-a-732-byte-python-script-gives-local-root-on-every-major-linux-distro-since-2017-and-cisa-orders-federal-agencies-to-patch-by-may-15) and [reported on](/article/2026-05/10-dirty-frag-a-second-linux-kernel-zero-day-in-five-weeks-hands-root-via-chained-esp-and-rxrpc-page-cache-bugs) as they emerged earlier this year. The Hacker News also reports a smaller, distinctive detail: "the agent's web interface password contains the Chinese word Leishen, thunder god."

On attribution, [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hacker-runs-hermes-ai-agent-unattended.html) reports that "Hunt.io assesses with low-to-medium confidence that the operator is Chinese-speaking or fluent in the language," without naming a specific intrusion group. Both outlets agree on two other points: [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/) reports that "the Ministry of Finance has not confirmed that its systems were breached," and that "Hunt says it found no evidence that these files were exfiltrated" — a finding [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hacker-runs-hermes-ai-agent-unattended.html) echoes, reporting that "nothing in the recovered files shows data leaving the network." Both outlets also report that Thailand's national CERT and cybersecurity agency were notified on July 15.

## What We Don't Know

Neither outlet names the intrusion group behind the operation, and the Ministry of Finance has not issued a public confirmation or denial of a breach. It also remains unclear how the attacker first gained access to the ministry's network before deploying Hermes, and whether the exposed staging server's history with ShadowPad and VShell malware ties this operation to a previously tracked campaign.

## Analysis

The episode is one of the more concrete public examples of an open-source AI agent being repurposed for unattended offensive operations against a government network, rather than as a proof-of-concept or lab demonstration. Because YOLO mode is a documented, built-in feature of Hermes rather than a vulnerability in it, the incident illustrates an operational choice by the attacker — disabling human-approval prompts — rather than a flaw the developers need to patch, underscoring a broader risk in how freely available agent frameworks can be configured for autonomous post-exploitation work once an attacker already has a foothold.
